questions.stem: Which quadrant of the chart best represents the views typically associated with modern American conservatives?
choices: Q
P
R
S
questions.explanation: Conservatives generally favor less government regulation of the economy but more support for traditional social values. Modern liberals generally favor more economic intervention and less social regulation, quadrant S.

questions.stem: Which policy position is most consistent with modern American liberalism?
choices: Reducing taxes and cutting social welfare spending
Eliminating most government programs
Restricting individual social choices to promote traditional values
Expanding government programs to reduce income inequality and increasing regulation of business
questions.explanation: Liberals generally see government as a tool to promote equality and address market failures, while conservatives emphasize individual responsibility and limited government in the economy.

questions.stem: During a recession, Congress cuts taxes and increases government spending. What type of policy is this, and which school of thought supports it?
choices: Expansionary fiscal policy, supported by Keynesian economics
Contractionary monetary policy, supported by supply-side economics
Expansionary monetary policy, set by Congress
Contractionary fiscal policy, supported by Keynesian economics
questions.explanation: Keynesians argue that government spending can boost demand when private spending falls. Fiscal policy is set by Congress and the president; monetary policy is set by the Federal Reserve.

questions.stem: Which institution controls monetary policy in the United States, and what is one of its main tools?
choices: Congress, which sets tax rates
The Treasury Department, which writes the federal budget
The Federal Reserve, which adjusts interest rates to influence borrowing and inflation
The Supreme Court, which reviews economic laws
questions.explanation: The Fed's independence is meant to insulate monetary decisions from short-term political pressure. Raising interest rates tends to slow inflation, while lowering them encourages borrowing.

questions.stem: Which policy is most associated with supply-side economics?
choices: Increasing government spending during recessions
Raising tax rates on high incomes to reduce inequality
Setting government price controls
Cutting tax rates, especially on businesses and investment, to encourage production and economic growth
questions.explanation: Supply-side advocates argue that lower taxes and less regulation increase incentives to work and invest. The approach was central to President Reagan's economic policy.

questions.stem: Libertarians are most likely to support which policy?
choices: Expanding government health care programs
Increasing restrictions on personal behavior
Reducing government regulation of both the economy and personal choices
Raising tariffs to protect domestic industries
questions.explanation: Libertarians prioritize individual liberty and limited government across both economic and social issues.

questions.stem: Which factor most often limits the influence of public opinion on specific policy decisions?
choices: Public opinion polls are illegal in election years.
Many citizens have little information about specific policies, and opinions on details are often unstable.
Elected officials are forbidden to consider polls.
Public opinion never changes.
questions.explanation: Officials respond to public opinion on salient issues, but on technical questions they are often guided by interest groups, experts, and party leaders.

questions.stem: Which change has most increased the variety of sources that shape Americans' political views?
choices: The growth of the internet and social media, which allows people to choose sources that match their views
The decline of public schools
The end of newspapers
The elimination of political parties
questions.explanation: Easy access to many sources can increase information but also allows selective exposure, contributing to polarization.

questions.stem: Which effect has globalization had on American political attitudes?
choices: It has eliminated disagreement over trade.
It has had no effect on public opinion.
It has increased debates over trade, immigration, and the effects of international competition on American workers.
It has caused all Americans to support free trade.
questions.explanation: Some voters have benefited from trade, while others, such as workers in some manufacturing industries, have faced job losses, shaping views across both parties.

questions.stem: What is an exit poll?
choices: A survey of voters as they leave polling places, used to predict outcomes and analyze voting patterns
A survey of people who chose not to vote
A count of ballots done by election officials
A poll that asks only about candidates who dropped out
questions.explanation: Exit polls help explain why people voted as they did by group. They can be inaccurate if certain voters, such as early or mail-in voters, are not surveyed.

questions.skill: Ideology and the role of government
questions.stem: Which statement best explains why liberals and conservatives often disagree about the size of government?
choices: They disagree about whether the Constitution exists.
Liberals oppose all government spending.
Conservatives oppose all government programs, including the military.
They hold different views about whether government action or private markets better promote individual well-being and equality.
questions.explanation: Both groups support some government functions. They disagree about the balance between individual responsibility, market outcomes, and public programs.

questions.stem: Which policy is typically favored by the Republican Party and opposed by the Democratic Party?
choices: Increasing the federal minimum wage
Lowering taxes and reducing federal regulation of business
Expanding federal health insurance programs
Increasing environmental regulation
questions.explanation: Party platforms reflect ideological differences, though both parties include a range of views.

questions.stem: A pollster conducts a "push poll." What is its purpose?
choices: To measure opinion accurately with neutral questions
To spread negative information about a candidate under the guise of asking questions
To predict election results after polls close
To test the opinions of experts
questions.explanation: Push polls are campaign tactics, not genuine surveys. Questions such as "Would you vote for X if you knew…" are designed to change opinions.

questions.stem: A citizen believes that voting does not matter because officials ignore people like them. Which concept does this describe?
choices: High political efficacy
Strong party identification
Rational choice voting
Low political efficacy
questions.explanation: Political efficacy is the belief that one can understand and influence politics. Low efficacy is associated with lower turnout.

questions.stem: Which source of data would give a researcher the most reliable measure of national public opinion on an issue?
choices: A scientific poll of a large, random, national sample with neutral question wording
Letters sent to members of Congress
Comments on a popular news website
Attendance at political rallies
questions.explanation: Letters, comments, and rallies reflect the views of the most motivated people. Random samples represent the whole population.

questions.stem: Which policy debate most directly reflects a tension between the values of individualism and equality of opportunity?
choices: Whether to hold elections every two years
Whether the president commands the military
Whether taxpayers should fund programs such as early-childhood education to help disadvantaged children compete
Whether states may coin money
questions.explanation: Supporters argue such programs make opportunity real; opponents may see them as an unwarranted expansion of government into individual and family responsibilities.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the differences between the parties on social policy?
choices: Both parties hold identical social policy positions.
Democrats oppose civil rights laws.
Republicans favor expanding all government programs.
Republicans generally emphasize traditional values and limits on some social changes, while Democrats generally emphasize expanding individual and civil rights protections.
questions.explanation: Issues such as abortion, gun policy, and immigration divide the parties' bases, though individuals within each party hold varied views.

questions.stem: Why do pollsters weight survey results?
choices: To change the results to favor one candidate
To reduce the size of the sample
To adjust the sample so that its demographic makeup matches that of the population
To eliminate the margin of error entirely
questions.explanation: If a sample has too few young respondents, for example, their answers are counted more heavily so that the results better reflect the whole population.

questions.stem: Why is the Federal Reserve designed to be independent of elected officials?
choices: So that it can set tax rates
So that monetary policy is based on long-term economic stability rather than short-term political pressures
So that it can write the federal budget
So that it can override Congress
questions.explanation: Elected officials might favor low interest rates before elections even if inflation results. Fed governors serve long, staggered terms.

questions.stem: Which group is most likely to favor a large role for government in regulating the economy but a limited role in regulating personal behavior?
choices: Liberals
Conservatives
Libertarians
Populists who oppose all regulation
questions.explanation: Liberals generally support economic regulation and social programs while emphasizing personal freedoms such as privacy.

questions.stem: Which statement best explains why Americans can share core values yet disagree sharply on policy?
choices: Americans do not share any core values.
Core values determine a single correct policy.
People interpret and prioritize shared values, such as liberty and equality, differently.
Disagreement occurs only among elected officials.
questions.explanation: Liberty may suggest lower taxes to one person and protection of civil liberties to another. Equality may mean equal treatment or more equal outcomes.

choices: Surveying the same people repeatedly over many decades
Surveying a single generation once
Asking only the oldest generation about its views
Counting the number of registered Democrats in one year
questions.explanation: A longitudinal panel shows whether people's views change as they age (life-cycle effects) or stay stable within each generation (generational effects).

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the relationship between public opinion and Supreme Court decisions?
choices: Justices must follow opinion polls.
Public opinion has no relationship to court decisions.
The Court must hold a referendum before major rulings.
Justices are not elected and are insulated from public opinion, but rulings can be shaped by and can shape public attitudes over time.
questions.explanation: Life tenure insulates the Court, but justices are aware that their legitimacy depends on public acceptance of their rulings.

questions.stem: Which development is most likely to shift public opinion on a social issue over time?
choices: A single opinion poll
Generational replacement, as younger people with different views replace older generations in the electorate
A new tax on businesses
A redistricting plan
questions.explanation: Attitudes toward issues such as same-sex marriage changed dramatically in part because younger cohorts held more accepting views than older ones.

questions.stem: Which amendment lowered the voting age to 18?
choices: The Nineteenth Amendment
The Twenty-sixth Amendment
The Twenty-fourth Amendment
The Fifteenth Amendment
questions.explanation: Ratified in 1971 during the Vietnam War, it was supported by the argument that people old enough to be drafted should be able to vote.

questions.stem: Which amendment prohibits poll taxes in federal elections?
choices: The Twenty-sixth Amendment
The Seventeenth Amendment
The Fifteenth Amendment
The Twenty-fourth Amendment
questions.explanation: Poll taxes had been used to keep poor and Black citizens from voting. The Supreme Court later extended the ban to state elections in Harper v. Virginia Board of Elections (1966).

questions.stem: Which conclusion about turnout and age is best supported by the graph?
choices: Turnout increases with age, with voters 65 and older more than 25 percentage points more likely to vote than those 18 to 24.
Young voters have the highest turnout.
Turnout is the same in all age groups.
Turnout decreases with age.
questions.explanation: Older citizens are more likely to be settled in a community, registered, and directly affected by programs such as Social Security. Young people move often and may not yet have the habit of voting.

questions.stem: Which policy would most likely narrow the gap in turnout shown in the graph?
choices: Requiring voters to register 60 days before an election
Moving elections to a weekday with no early voting
Automatic or same-day voter registration
Requiring a fee to vote
questions.explanation: Registration requirements are a major barrier for young, mobile citizens. Lowering such barriers tends to raise turnout among groups with lower participation.

choices: Turnout is higher in odd-numbered years.
Turnout increases steadily over time.
Midterm elections receive more media attention.
Turnout is much higher in presidential election years than in midterm election years.
questions.explanation: Presidential races are more visible and competitive and receive more media coverage, so more people vote. Midterm electorates are older and more partisan.

questions.stem: How many percentage points higher was turnout in the 2020 presidential election than in the 2022 midterm, according to the graph?
choices: \(46\) percentage points
\(20\) percentage points
\(66\) percentage points
questions.explanation: \(66-46=20\) percentage points. Relative to the midterm turnout, presidential turnout was about \(43\%\) higher, a different measure.

questions.stem: A voter supports the incumbent president because the economy improved during the past four years. Which model of voting behavior does this illustrate?
choices: Prospective voting
Retrospective voting
Party-line voting
Rational choice based on future promises
questions.explanation: Retrospective voters judge officials on past performance. Prospective voters choose based on predictions of future policy.

questions.stem: A voter supports every candidate of one party on the ballot, regardless of the office. Which model does this illustrate?
choices: Party-line voting
Retrospective voting
Split-ticket voting
Prospective voting
questions.explanation: Party identification provides a shortcut for voters with limited information. Split-ticket voting, choosing candidates of different parties, has declined as polarization has increased.

questions.stem: Which model of voting describes a citizen who compares candidates' positions and votes for the one whose policies best serve the citizen's own interests?
choices: Party-line voting
Retrospective voting
Rational-choice voting
Habitual voting
questions.explanation: Rational-choice voters weigh the costs and benefits of each candidate's policies for themselves.

questions.stem: Which is a primary function of political parties in the United States?
choices: Recruiting candidates, mobilizing voters, and organizing government
Writing the Constitution
Appointing federal judges
Conducting the census
questions.explanation: Parties nominate candidates, help voters make decisions, raise money, and organize Congress through party leadership and committee assignments.

questions.stem: Which feature of the U.S. electoral system most limits the success of third parties?
choices: Proportional representation in Congress
Public financing of all candidates
Direct election of the president by popular vote
Single-member districts with winner-take-all, plurality elections
questions.explanation: A party that wins 15 percent of the vote in every district may win no seats. Voters may also see a third-party vote as wasted.

questions.stem: Third parties rarely win national elections. Which is their most common effect on American politics?
choices: Controlling Congress
Raising issues that major parties later adopt, and sometimes influencing election outcomes
Winning the presidency regularly
Eliminating one of the major parties
questions.explanation: Ideas such as the progressive income tax and direct election of senators were promoted by third parties before major parties adopted them.

questions.stem: Which describes a critical election that produces a party realignment?
choices: An election with very low turnout
An election that shifts the coalitions supporting the major parties, producing a new, lasting pattern of party control
A close election decided by recount
An election in which a third party wins the presidency
questions.explanation: The election of 1932, which built the New Deal coalition, is a classic example. Realignments reshape party coalitions for decades.

questions.stem: Why do interest groups representing broad public interests, such as clean air, often find it harder to organize than groups representing narrow interests?
choices: Because broad interests are illegal.
Because narrow groups are prohibited from lobbying.
Because members of broad groups cannot vote.
Because of the free-rider problem: people can enjoy the benefits without contributing to the group.
questions.explanation: Groups offer selective benefits, such as magazines or discounts, to overcome free riding. Small groups with concentrated stakes find it easier to organize.

questions.stem: Which is an example of lobbying by an interest group?
choices: Meeting with members of Congress and their staff to provide information and advocate for a bill
Voting in a primary election
Issuing an executive order
Deciding a court case
questions.explanation: Lobbyists provide expertise and information. Groups also file amicus curiae briefs, testify at hearings, and mobilize members.

questions.stem: An interest group files an amicus curiae brief in a Supreme Court case. What is its purpose?
choices: To serve as the defendant in the case
To appoint a justice to hear the case
To present arguments and information to persuade the justices, even though the group is not a party to the case
To appeal the decision to Congress
questions.explanation: Amicus briefs let groups influence the courts. Groups such as the NAACP have also sponsored test cases to change the law.

A super PAC cannot coordinate with candidates, has no contribution limits, and must disclose donors. A 501(c)(4) social welfare group cannot coordinate with candidates, has no contribution limits, and generally does not have to disclose donors

questions.stem: Which group in the table may spend unlimited money on political ads without disclosing its donors?
choices: A political action committee
A super PAC
A candidate's campaign committee
A 501(c)(4) social welfare group
questions.explanation: Such groups, a source of "dark money," may engage in political activity as long as it is not their primary purpose. Super PACs may raise unlimited money but must disclose donors.

A super PAC cannot coordinate with candidates, has no contribution limits, and must disclose donors. A 501(c)(4) social welfare group cannot coordinate with candidates, has no contribution limits, and generally does not have to disclose donors

questions.stem: Which Supreme Court decision made the growth of super PACs shown in the table possible?
choices: Buckley v. Valeo (1976)
Baker v. Carr (1962)
Citizens United v. Federal Election Commission (2010)
Marbury v. Madison (1803)
questions.explanation: The Court held that limits on independent political spending by corporations and unions violate the First Amendment. Lower courts then struck down contribution limits for independent-expenditure groups.

questions.stem: Which reasoning did the Supreme Court majority use in Citizens United v. FEC?
choices: Corporations are not protected by the Constitution.
Independent spending on political speech by corporations and unions is protected by the First Amendment and does not give rise to corruption.
Spending money has nothing to do with speech.
Congress may ban all political advertising.
questions.explanation: Critics argue that the decision increased the influence of wealthy interests in elections. Direct contributions to candidates remain limited.

questions.stem: Which was a main goal of the Bipartisan Campaign Reform Act of 2002 (McCain-Feingold)?
choices: Banning unlimited "soft money" contributions to national political parties
Eliminating all campaign contributions
Requiring public financing for all candidates
Abolishing the Federal Election Commission
questions.explanation: Soft money had been raised for party-building activities but often used to support candidates. Citizens United struck down other parts of the law limiting corporate election ads.

figure.alt: Table of a hypothetical presidential election result. Candidate X: 50.4 percent of the popular vote, 22 states, 260 electoral votes. Candidate Y: 48.1 percent, 28 states, 278 electoral votes. Others: 1.5 percent, no states, no electoral votes

questions.stem: Which statement correctly explains the result shown in the table?
choices: Candidate X won because of the popular vote.
No candidate won because neither had 270 electoral votes.
Candidate Y won the presidency with a majority of electoral votes, although Candidate X won more popular votes.
The House chose the winner because no candidate won a majority of the popular vote.
questions.explanation: A candidate needs 270 of 538 electoral votes. Because nearly all states award all of their electors to the statewide winner, a candidate can win the Electoral College while losing the national popular vote.

questions.stem: Which feature of the Electoral College encourages presidential candidates to focus on a small number of states?
choices: Winner-take-all allocation of electoral votes in nearly every state, which makes competitive "swing states" decisive
The proportional allocation of electoral votes in every state
Direct popular election of the president
The requirement that candidates visit every state
questions.explanation: Candidates have little reason to campaign in states that reliably favor one party, so swing states receive most of the attention and spending.

questions.stem: Which conclusion about incumbents is best supported by the graph?
choices: Senate incumbents always lose.
House incumbents win fewer than half of their races.
Incumbency makes no difference to election outcomes.
Incumbents seeking reelection usually win, and House incumbents have generally been reelected at higher rates than Senate incumbents.
questions.explanation: Incumbency advantages include name recognition, fundraising, constituent service, and favorable districts. Senate races are often more competitive because states are larger and more diverse than House districts.

questions.stem: Which advantage do House incumbents have over challengers?
choices: Guaranteed reelection under the Constitution
Name recognition, franking privileges, a record of constituent service, and an easier time raising money
The right to choose their opponents
Longer terms than senators
questions.explanation: Gerrymandered safe seats add to the advantage. Challengers typically raise far less money.

questions.stem: How does a closed primary differ from an open primary?
choices: Closed primaries are held after the general election.
Only voters registered with a party may vote in its closed primary, while any registered voter may vote in an open primary.
Open primaries choose the president directly.
Closed primaries allow anyone to vote.
questions.explanation: Closed primaries tend to produce candidates who appeal to the party's base. Open primaries allow independents and members of other parties to participate.

questions.stem: Which change in the presidential nomination process since the 1970s has given voters more influence?
choices: The abolition of national conventions
The elimination of superdelegates in both parties
The selection of nominees by Congress
The widespread use of primaries and caucuses to choose delegates, rather than selection by party leaders
questions.explanation: Reforms after 1968 shifted power from party leaders to rank-and-file voters. Candidates now must campaign intensively in early states such as Iowa and New Hampshire.

questions.stem: Which describes "horse-race" journalism?
choices: Coverage that focuses on who is ahead in polls and campaign strategy rather than candidates' policy positions
Investigative reporting on government corruption
Coverage of sporting events
Editorials endorsing candidates
questions.explanation: Critics argue that horse-race coverage leaves voters less informed about the issues, though it attracts audiences.

questions.stem: Which effect of social media and partisan news on political participation concerns many scholars?
choices: A sharp decline in the availability of political information
An end to campaign advertising
Echo chambers, in which people see mainly information that confirms their views, increasing polarization
Equal coverage of all candidates
questions.explanation: Algorithms and personal choices can narrow the range of viewpoints people encounter. Social media also allows rapid spread of misinformation.

questions.stem: Which role of the news media is often called "watchdog" journalism?
choices: Selecting which candidates appear on the ballot
Writing legislation
Conducting official election counts
Investigating and exposing wrongdoing by government officials
questions.explanation: Investigative reporting, such as coverage of Watergate, holds officials accountable. The media also act as gatekeepers, deciding which stories receive attention.

questions.stem: Which factor most helped the women's suffrage movement achieve ratification of the Nineteenth Amendment in 1920?
choices: A Supreme Court ruling requiring women's suffrage
An executive order by the president
Decades of organizing, protests, and state-level victories, along with women's contributions during World War I
A decision by party conventions
questions.explanation: Several western states had granted women the vote before 1920. Sustained pressure built support in Congress and the state legislatures for the amendment.

questions.stem: Which of the following are linkage institutions that connect citizens to government?
choices: Congress, the president, and the courts
Political parties, interest groups, elections, and the media
The Bill of Rights and the Constitution
The Federal Reserve and the Treasury
questions.explanation: Linkage institutions channel public preferences to policymakers. The three branches are the institutions of government itself.

questions.stem: Which demographic factor is most strongly associated with higher voter turnout?
choices: Higher levels of education
Younger age
Lower income
Recent change of residence
questions.explanation: Education increases knowledge of politics, political efficacy, and familiarity with registration procedures. Income and age are also positively associated with turnout.

questions.stem: Supporters of strict voter ID laws argue that they prevent fraud. What do opponents most often argue?
choices: They increase turnout among all groups.
They are required by the Constitution.
They impose burdens that fall disproportionately on poor, elderly, and minority voters, who are less likely to have ID, while in-person fraud is extremely rare.
They apply only to federal judges.
questions.explanation: The debate reflects the tension between protecting the integrity of elections and ensuring access to voting.

questions.stem: Why have the two major parties become more ideologically polarized in recent decades?
choices: Partisan sorting, safe districts, primary elections that reward appealing to the base, and polarized media
The elimination of primary elections
The rise of a strong third party
A constitutional amendment requiring polarization
questions.explanation: Conservatives have increasingly sorted into the Republican Party and liberals into the Democratic Party, reducing the overlap between the parties in Congress.

questions.stem: How has the internet changed the way campaigns operate?
choices: It has eliminated the need to raise money.
It has banned television advertising.
It requires candidates to debate online.
It allows candidates to raise small donations from many supporters and target messages to specific groups of voters.
questions.explanation: Online fundraising and microtargeted ads have made campaigns less dependent on party organizations and large donors, while raising concerns about privacy and misinformation.

questions.stem: Which describes the "revolving door" between government and interest groups?
choices: Interest groups are banned from contacting officials.
Former government officials take jobs as lobbyists, and lobbyists take positions in government.
Members of Congress must rotate committees each term.
Voters move between political parties frequently.
questions.explanation: Critics argue that the revolving door gives some interests special access. Federal law imposes waiting periods before former officials may lobby their old agencies.

questions.stem: Which strategy did the civil rights and environmental movements both use to influence policy?
choices: Relying only on electing their own third-party presidents
Mobilizing public opinion through protests and media attention while lobbying and litigating for change
Avoiding all contact with government
Using only the amendment process
questions.explanation: Social movements combine grassroots activism with institutional strategies. Earth Day in 1970 built support for the Clean Air Act and the creation of the EPA.

questions.stem: The Fifteenth Amendment prohibited denying the vote on the basis of race. Why did many Black Southerners remain unable to vote until the 1960s?
choices: The amendment applied only to Northern states.
The Supreme Court declared the amendment unconstitutional.
Congress repealed the amendment.
States used poll taxes, literacy tests, white primaries, and intimidation to keep them from voting.
questions.explanation: The Twenty-fourth Amendment and the Voting Rights Act of 1965 dismantled these barriers.

questions.stem: Besides voting, which is a form of political participation?
choices: Contributing to a campaign, contacting officials, or participating in a protest
Paying sales tax
Receiving a passport
Attending public school
questions.explanation: Participation includes any activity that seeks to influence government. Different forms require different amounts of time, money, and skill.

questions.stem: What happens if no presidential candidate wins a majority of the electoral votes?
choices: The candidate with the most popular votes wins.
The Supreme Court chooses the president.
The House of Representatives chooses the president, with each state delegation casting one vote.
The Senate chooses the president with each senator casting one vote.
questions.explanation: Under the Twelfth Amendment, the House chooses among the top three candidates, and the Senate chooses the vice president.
